text: It's an old classic point and click adventure game, which means lots of nonsensical puzzles and 'moon logic', although for its time it actually had more logical puzzles in an effort to try and save a dying genre. Today however, after the genre's renewal through the indie game scene, it is still terribly illogical and has lots of annoying backtracking compared to modern point and clicks like Fran Bow. So in today's era of large Steam backlogs, unless you want to waste your precious time brute force combining items until you hit the right combo and the story moves on, grabbing a walkthrough is highly recommended. I kept playing and eventually completed it, using a walkthrough of course, because I'm interested in the Aztec/Mexican/Mesoamerican death folklore.  It is understandable if you give up long before reaching that point, as even with this being a remaster, almost everything is terrible. For example apart from the gameplay mentioned above, the controls change direction when you enter a new location, the pre-rendered graphics of the cinematics have artifacts and are in lower resolution than what you are probably playing at, ... and so on. title: guardians of middle-earth
text: In a world where dota and league of legends have firmly planted their flag in the moba genre, you would either have to be a revolutionary game designer or a complete idiot to try to compete with them. In this case, Guardians of Middle-earth and their respective no-name developer team falls flat on its face in the latter category. The only way I could rationalize the developer's strategy for releasing this game is that this game was designed for five year olds. Gold mechanic too hard? Ok we removed it. Dota's 25 level cap too hard? LoL's 18? Ok we made it 14. Mana management too difficult? We got rid of that too. In this dumbed down world, you max out your level in about ten minutes, but with no gold, you will never get an edge on your opponent. In an hour, you will be sitting there, everyone maxed at 14, praying something happens. In this joke of a world where some random hobbit can 1v1 the lord of Mordor himself, the biggest enemy to both teams is boredom. I highly suspect that there's a payment scheme of somewhat that I would balk at, but honestly, if you can't retain a player for ten minutes, then whatever crafty method you devised for generating is the least of your problems. The single redeeming factor of the game was the portraits of the characters in character selection. They were very artful, and I could only pray the graphic designers weren't tortured with seeing what mangled sprites their art was attached to. Do not buy this game, do not recommend this game, do not talk about this game. It was free, and I still feel cheated for the time I spent playing it. I hope that whoever thought of this game still has an in with the production team of lord of the rings, because he is not going to make it as a video game developer.

title: guns of icarus online
text: This game is, mechanically, one of the best on Steam. It's great. However, there is one overarching problem with it; A relatively small playerbase. This can result in high-ping games and half-full servers, which is a major blow to the game. The only way we can fix this problem is by playing the game. It's a good game, so it can't be that hard. I suppose this is due to a fairly rough initial learning curve. Aside from the small playerbase and the resulting issues, this is a niche but very entertaining game. Let me break it down: -This is a four-player coop, ignore any other category. If you loved the interplay and teamwork of working with a small team, such as playing Payday 2 or Left 4 Dead 2, then you should really look at Guns of Icarus. Teamwork is critical to the game and if that's what you love, you will love this game. -Artwork. The art alone is reason to buy the game. This game has the best artwork I've ever seen in any game. Ever. Hands down. Music's bloody good too. Graphics and animations are pretty average, but the sheer coolness of crewing the GoI warships willl guarantee you get your money's worth just exploring the game. The fast paces (often exceeding 100 k/h) of the airships and heavy damage taken constantly from a damage-centered gameplay dynamic serve to remind you at every second that you're riding not a modern airliner or a fireproofed helium blimp - these ships are slap-dash and falling apart around you, but this only serves to create a thrilling atmosphere in combat as parts go flying and clouds of smoke throw you into the shoes of a reckless young sailor with nothing left to lose, Not fighting for his life so much as throwing whatever he, his ship and his crew have left in the all-pervading pursuit of victory.
